Resting EEG band power in adolescents with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders

Jennifer Hsieh, PhD

October 2026

Question

Is resting, eyes-closed EEG spectral power different in adolescents with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders compared with healthy adolescents, in which frequency bands and where on the scalp, and how well do these differences separate the two groups out of sample?

Data

The MSU adolescent schizophrenia EEG database (Borisov et al., 2005): 39 healthy schoolboys and 45 boys with schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses (ICD-10 F20, F21, F25), aged about 11 to 14, unmedicated at the time of recording. Each record is 60 s of wakeful, eyes-closed EEG from 16 scalp electrodes (10-20 system, linked-ear reference), sampled at 128 Hz and supplied as artefact-free segments. Source: http://brain.bio.msu.ru/eeg_schizophrenia.htm.

Methods

Cleaning and QC. Each channel was mean-centred. Recordings were checked for missing values and flat channels (none). The 60 s were split into 29 overlapping 4-s segments, and a segment was rejected if any channel’s peak-to-peak amplitude exceeded that channel’s within-subject median + 5 MAD. Median rejected segments per subject: 0 (max 4 of 29), so no subject met the pre-specified exclusion rule (> 25% rejected). 7 channel recordings had outlying overall variance (|robust z| > 3.5, from 2 subjects); they were kept, because log band power absorbs gain differences and the data were supplied as clean.

Spectra and features. Welch PSD per channel (4-s Hann windows, 50% overlap, linear detrend, 0.25 Hz resolution). Band power was integrated over delta (1-4 Hz), theta (4-8), alpha (8-13) and beta (13-30), and expressed as log10 absolute power and relative power (share of 1-30 Hz). Individual alpha peak frequency was the maximum of the mean posterior spectrum (O1, O2, P3, P4, Pz) between 7 and 13 Hz, refined by parabolic interpolation; 2 adolescents whose maximum sat on the 7 Hz edge (no identifiable peak) were left out of that test.

Statistics. For each of 16 channels x 4 bands x 2 measures: Welch t-test, with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test as a robustness check, and Hedges’ g with 95% CI (schizophrenia minus control). P-values were corrected with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR within each measure (64 tests). For a region-level view, a linear mixed model per band, log10 power ~ group * region + (1 | subject) (sum contrasts, Type III, Satterthwaite df; lmerTest).

Classifier. Elastic-net logistic regression (glmnet, alpha = 0.5) on all 128 band-power features, with lambda chosen by inner 5-fold CV inside each outer training fold (nested CV; standardisation learned on the training fold only). Performance: 10 x repeated stratified 5-fold CV. Baseline: logistic regression on one feature, mean relative alpha across channels. Significance: 200 label permutations of the full pipeline.

Results

Power spectra

The healthy group shows the expected posterior alpha peak; in the schizophrenia group it is lower and shifted to slower frequencies, while delta and theta power look similar.

Channel-by-band effect sizes

Measure Band Channels FDR q<.05 (t-test) Channels FDR q<.05 (Wilcoxon) Hedges g range
Log absolute delta 0 0 -0.13 to 0.35
Log absolute theta 0 0 -0.27 to 0.29
Log absolute alpha 12 14 -1.02 to -0.15
Log absolute beta 1 3 -0.60 to -0.09
Relative delta 13 7 0.37 to 1.05
Relative theta 9 4 0.20 to 0.82
Relative alpha 15 15 -1.25 to -0.41
Relative beta 0 1 -0.29 to 0.45
  • Alpha is reduced in schizophrenia: lower absolute alpha at 12 of 16 channels and lower relative alpha at 15 of 16. The largest effect is relative alpha at O1 (g = -1.25, 95% CI -1.72 to -0.78).
  • Absolute delta and theta do not differ (all |g| < 0.36, none significant), so the higher relative delta and theta in schizophrenia mostly reflects the smaller alpha share, not extra slow-wave power. The relative delta/theta effects are less robust to the rank-based test.
  • Beta trends lower in absolute terms (one channel, P3, survives FDR).

Only alpha shows a main effect of group after FDR. Group x region interactions are significant in every band, i.e. the group difference is not uniform over the scalp: for alpha it is largest over occipital and frontal sites, where the schizophrenia group has roughly 45-60% of control alpha power.

Alpha peak frequency

Mean alpha peak was 9.83 Hz (SD 0.70) in controls and 9.26 Hz (SD 0.86) in the schizophrenia group: Welch t(79.2) = -3.28, p = 0.002, g = -0.71 [-1.16, -0.26].

Classification

Model AUC mean (range over repeats) Balanced accuracy Permutation p
Baseline: global relative alpha 0.76 (0.74-0.77) 0.65
Elastic net (128 features) 0.79 (0.72-0.83) 0.71 0.005

The elastic net reached a cross-validated AUC of 0.79, well above the permutation null (95th percentile 0.55; none of 200 permutations reached the observed value), but only slightly better than the single global-relative-alpha feature (AUC 0.76). The most consistently selected features were rel_alpha_O1, rel_alpha_O2, rel_alpha_F3, abs_log10_alpha_F4, rel_delta_O1: alpha again carries most of the signal.

Interpretation

Unmedicated adolescents with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders show a reduced and slower alpha rhythm at rest, with otherwise similar absolute slow-wave power. This sits alongside the original authors’ report, in this same sample, of altered alpha-segment structure and reduced structural synchrony of alpha activity; here the effect shows up in plain spectral power as well. A spectral signature like this separates groups at roughly 70% balanced accuracy, which is useful for research but nowhere near a diagnostic test.

Limitations

  • Small, single-site, all-male sample from one 2005 database; no age, IQ or symptom data per subject, so age (which strongly shapes alpha frequency in adolescence) cannot be modelled directly. The authors report matched mean ages (12.3 years in both groups).
  • 60 s per subject; recordings were pre-selected as artefact-free by the data providers.
  • The amplitude scale in the files is larger than typical scalp EEG in microvolts, so absolute power is reported on a log scale and interpreted only relative to the other group; relative power and peak frequency are unaffected by gain.
  • 50 Hz is barely visible in the spectra, which suggests the data were low-pass filtered before sharing; analysis was restricted to 1-30 Hz.
  • No licence is stated on the source page; the data are not redistributed here.

Reference

Borisov SV, Kaplan AYa, Gorbachevskaya NL, Kozlova IA (2005). Analysis of EEG structural synchrony in adolescents with schizophrenic disorders. Human Physiology 31(3):255-261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10747-005-0042-z
